description_ru: Выдуманная новость о двух соседних деревнях, которые три века спорили о церковном колоколе, и о неожиданной развязке на мировом суде.
text:
UPPER GRAYLING AND NETHER GRAYLING, Westmarch. After three hundred and eleven years of litigation, vendetta, pamphleteering and one memorable incident involving a wheelbarrow, the neighbouring villages of Upper Grayling and Nether Grayling have agreed to share a bell. The settlement, brokered on Friday in the draughty hall of the district magistrates' court, brings to an end what local historians have called the longest-running dispute over a piece of metal in the western hemisphere, and has left both parties feeling, according to one observer, "equally and exquisitely dissatisfied."

The bell, a bronze object weighing slightly more than a grand piano, was cast in 1713 by a founder named Josiah Pennywhistle, who inscribed upon it a Latin motto of such obscurity that scholars have been quarrelling over its meaning for almost as long as the villages have been quarrelling over its ownership. It hung in a church tower that stood, by an unhappy accident of medieval surveying, exactly upon the boundary between the two parishes, so that the nave lay in Upper Grayling, the belfry in Nether Grayling and the vestry, in which the tea was kept, in a sort of constitutional no man's land.

The trouble began, as all great troubles do, with a matter of etiquette. In the summer of 1714, the bell rang for the wedding of a Nether Grayling farmer's daughter, and the people of Upper Grayling, who had lent the bride a cow, felt that the peal had been rung in a notably ungrateful key. Words were exchanged. Over the following three centuries, the bell was twice stolen, once ransomed, thrice lost in a flood and, in 1887, buried in a field in a fit of pique by an elderly sexton, who forgot where he had put it and went to his grave without admitting as much.

Each village, meanwhile, developed an elaborate mythology of grievance. In Upper Grayling, children grew up believing that their neighbours had hidden the clapper in a cheese; in Nether Grayling, it was an article of faith that the people upstream had taught their cattle to trample the hedges. Annual festivals were organised in which an effigy of the opposing village was solemnly paraded through the streets, and then, because the villagers were fundamentally kind-hearted, given a slice of cake and a seat by the fire.

The legal history is, if anything, more bewildering. Over the centuries the dispute has occupied nineteen courts, produced eight royal commissions and generated a bulk of documents so vast that the Westmarch County Archive has been obliged to reinforce its floor. One judge, in 1792, ruled that the bell belonged to the church; another, in 1841, ruled that the church belonged to the bell; and a third, in 1936, was said to have retired to a monastery rather than hear the matter again. A solicitor from Nether Grayling, Mr Barnaby Strickland-Eze, has described the case as "the only inheritance that three generations of my family have received in full."

Peace arrived, at last, from an unexpected quarter. Last winter, a youthful magistrate, Miss Clementine Oduya-Whitlock, newly appointed and possessed of an unfashionable faith in common sense, visited both villages in the course of preparing her judgment. She found, to her surprise, that the inhabitants of both places had been intermarrying for generations, that most of them were cousins, and that a considerable number attended the same pub, the Bell and Cleaver, which stands, with an irony that has escaped no one, on the exact boundary line.

"It dawned on me," she told reporters, "that the two villages did not truly hate each other. They merely lacked an excuse to stop." Her solution, which she unveiled on Friday with the air of a conjuror, is a masterpiece of diplomatic ambiguity. The bell will be rung on alternate days by the two parishes; it will be rung on the hour by Upper Grayling and on the half-hour by Nether Grayling; and on Sundays it will be rung jointly, by a team of four from each village, who must, by order of the court, share a single rope and a flask of cider.

The ruling was received with a silence so complete that, for a moment, a clerk feared that the acoustics of the hall had failed. Then an elderly farmer rose in the gallery, looked at the representative of the opposing village, and said, "Well, I suppose that would be all right." This remark, according to witnesses, caused a collective exhalation that was audible as far as the car park, and the villagers, to their evident astonishment, found that they were shaking hands.

Not everyone is satisfied. The Grayling Historical Society, whose entire reason for being is the dispute, has issued an anguished statement lamenting "the vandalism of resolution." The local newspaper, the Grayling Gazette, which has sold copies on the strength of the feud since 1802, has been obliged to rethink its front page, and has announced a series entitled Cheese: Is It Time to Talk? Meanwhile, a rival band of bell-ringers from a village nine miles away has already declared an interest in the clapper, and has been told to wait its turn.

For the moment, there is a certain wariness in the lanes. The rule that the bell must be rung together on Sundays has produced what a spokesman for the diocese described as "an unprecedented outbreak of rhythm," as eight men, pulling on one rope, discovered that it is considerably easier to produce a beautiful sound if everyone agrees when to pull. At the first joint peal, on Sunday morning, the bell rang out across the water meadows with a note so deep and clean that the cows, who had been grazing contentedly on the boundary, raised their heads as one.

Afterwards, in the Bell and Cleaver, the two teams stood at the bar and fell into an awkward silence, which was ended by the landlord, who observed that they all appeared to have forgotten the original quarrel. "Oh, I haven't forgotten it," said a man from Upper Grayling. "It was about a cow." "No, it wasn't," said a man from Nether Grayling. "It was about the key." They considered this, in the manner of people who have found a pleasant new subject, and ordered another round.

questions.question: What object did the two villages quarrel over?
In what year was the bell cast?
How will the bell be rung on Sundays?
questions.answer: Jointly by teams from both villages, sharing one rope.
